title: Indian Diaspora Rallies Behind CJP Protest Movement With Food, Funds and Online Solidarity
excerpt: As the Cockroach Janta Party's youth-led protests escalate in Delhi, Indians abroad are ordering meals to the Jantar Mantar site via delivery apps, amplifying the movement digitally and drawing international media attention to India's biggest Gen Z uprising.
body:
• Indians abroad are using Swiggy and Zomato to send meals, water and snacks to CJP protesters at Delhi's Jantar Mantar, with delivery riders reporting orders "from Kerala to the USA"
  • CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, a Boston University graduate who flew back from the US to lead the movement, embodies the diaspora connection driving the protests
  • The movement has drawn front-page coverage from The New York Times, The Guardian, BBC and CNN, amplifying NRI engagement as nationwide protests were called for Friday

Diaspora Turns Delivery Apps Into Protest Tools

From thousands of miles away, Indians living overseas have found a way to stand on the frontlines of India's biggest youth-led protest in over a decade — by ordering food.

https://x.com/JethmalaniM/status/2079735004259889429

A steady stream of delivery riders on motorcycles has been weaving through Delhi's traffic to ferry meals, bottled water and snacks to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest camp at Jantar Mantar, many of the orders placed by supporters across India and abroad who cannot physically join the demonstrations.

"From Kerala to the USA, orders are coming from everywhere."

— Suraj Kumar, 25, delivery rider at the protest site

So many meals poured in that organisers eventually issued an appeal asking people to stop sending further contributions, according to Reuters. The phenomenon mirrors tactics used during Indonesia's 2025 protest movement, where supporters in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand ordered food for demonstrators via apps.

Raj Rathore, a 25-year-old volunteer distributing deliveries at the site, told Reuters: "People are angry, especially after the police started beating innocent students. But not everyone can come here so they are sending food."

A Boston-to-Delhi Pipeline

The diaspora's connection to the CJP runs deeper than food orders. The movement's founder, Abhijeet Dipke, was based in Boston until early June, when he flew back to India to launch the first physical protest at Jantar Mantar. A digital communications strategist and Boston University graduate, Dipke built the CJP's online infrastructure using AI tools and meme-driven political messaging honed during a stint with the Aam Aadmi Party's social media team.

Within days of its May 16 launch — triggered by Chief Justice Surya Kant's widely criticised remarks calling unemployed youth "cockroaches" — the CJP had overtaken the BJP's official Instagram following and attracted tens of millions of supporters online. The hashtag #MainBhiCockroach trended across platforms, with NRIs among the most vocal amplifiers.

The movement's demands centre on the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over leaked NEET medical entrance exam papers that affected some 2 million students in May. Millions were forced to re-sit the exam.

Wangchuk Ends Fast, Protests Continue

On Thursday, activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a 26-day hunger strike after negotiations with two federal ministers, saying on X that he broke his fast "at the urging of scores of members of parliament" and following "a long negotiation on various conditions." He promised to detail the talks in a video.

CJP founder Dipke thanked Wangchuk for his "courage and sacrifice" but made clear the demonstrations would press on. "We won't let Sonam sir's sacrifice go in vain," he said in a video message.

Earlier Thursday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi made his first public response to the crisis, announcing that special courts would be set up to prosecute those behind exam paper leaks. "Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth!" he posted on X.

"But Modi-ji, tell us why are paper leaks happening in this country in the first place? Fast-track courts are set up in this country for every other issue, but whether those fast-track courts have actually solved those issues — you know the answer to that question, and so do we."

— Ashutosh Ranka, CJP spokesperson

International Spotlight Intensifies NRI Engagement

The protests have drawn sustained front-page coverage from major international outlets including The New York Times, The Guardian, BBC and CNN, which described the CJP as "a youth-led movement that began as a joke but has since grown into a political force." The Associated Press called it "a major outlet for youth anger."

That global visibility has fuelled diaspora involvement. On social media, NRIs have organised fundraising campaigns, shared protest footage and coordinated solidarity messaging. The movement's digital-first architecture — built on Instagram, X and WhatsApp — has made it unusually accessible to Indians overseas who may feel disconnected from traditional Indian political movements.

Top Bollywood stars including Salman Khan, Alia Bhatt, Kareena Kapoor, Diljit Dosanjh and dozens of others have also backed the protesters via social media, further expanding the movement's reach among the diaspora.

What's Next

The CJP has called nationwide protests for Friday, even as the government shut down mobile internet services within a 1.5-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar and closed 16 Delhi Metro stations in central areas. Modi said a cabinet meeting on Friday would announce stricter measures against paper leaks.

The movement has spread well beyond Delhi, with demonstrations reported in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata, Pune, Ranchi, Thiruvananthapuram and several other cities. Opposition parties, including Congress, Samajwadi Party and Trinamool Congress, have rallied behind the students, disrupting parliament's monsoon session.

For the estimated 32 million Indians living abroad, many of whom navigated India's competitive exam system themselves, the CJP's fight over exam integrity strikes a deeply personal chord — one they are increasingly finding ways to act on from afar.
image_caption: Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, the epicenter of the CJP protests where diaspora-ordered food deliveries have been arriving from overseas
nri_angle: Indians abroad are supporting the CJP protest movement through food delivery app orders, online solidarity campaigns, and social media amplification, with the movement's US-based founder embodying the diaspora connection.
author: Diaspora Desk
